issues.legal_issue: A tenant protected by rent-control law retains that status when an attempted fresh lease is ineffective for want of registration and does not become a trespasser merely because the attempted lease term expires.
material_facts: The company was accepted as a tenant and was in possession before the parties attempted to create a fresh five-year tenancy.
The premises were governed by rent-control legislation when the earlier contractual tenancy expired, and the company continued in possession under its protection.
The fresh lease was not registered, and the company was not put into possession under that purported lease.
The landlords accepted rent from the company, and the company neither surrendered possession nor was evicted through legal proceedings; the landlords instead locked part of the premises.
issues.conclusion: The ineffective fresh lease did not alter the company's existing tenant status. It continued as a protected tenant and could be removed only in due course of law under the applicable rent-control legislation.
issues.legal_principle: On expiry of a contractual tenancy, a tenant protected by rent-control legislation has the statutory status of irremovability and remains protected until surrender or eviction under the legislation. An ineffective, unregistered attempt to create a fresh lease does not destroy the status of a person who was already a tenant and was not put into possession under that lease. The Court relied on Anand Nivas P. Ltd. v. Anandji Kalyanji Pedhi, [1964] 4 SCR 892, and Hiralal Vallabhram v. Kastorbhai Lalbhai, [1967] 3 SCR 343; it considered the West Bengal Premises Rent Control (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950, and the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956.

rule.if: rent_control_tenancy_dispute and prior_tenant_status and rent_protection_applies and purported_fresh_lease_unregistered and tenant_remained_in_possession and not possession_surrendered and not lawful_eviction

predicates.rent_control_tenancy_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether an occupant of premises governed by rent-control law retains tenant status after a purported tenancy arrangement ends.
predicates.prior_tenant_status: The occupant was accepted as a tenant and was in possession before the purported fresh lease began.
predicates.rent_protection_applies: Rent-control legislation protected the occupant when the earlier contractual tenancy ended.
predicates.purported_fresh_lease_unregistered: The parties attempted a fresh lease requiring registration, but it was not registered.
predicates.tenant_remained_in_possession: The occupant continued in possession after the earlier tenancy ended.
predicates.possession_surrendered: The occupant gave up possession of the premises.
predicates.lawful_eviction: The occupant was evicted through legal proceedings under the applicable law.

issues.definition: When the proceeding concerns rent-controlled premises, a previously accepted tenant remains protected if the fresh lease was unregistered and the tenant stayed in possession without surrendering it or being lawfully evicted.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant may sue for a declaration of tenant status and for an injunction to protect possession against a landlord's interference.
material_facts: The company claimed that it continued to be a tenant after the purported fresh lease failed for want of registration.
The landlords locked a portion of the premises, and the company sought a declaration of its tenant status and injunctions against interference and to remove the locks.
issues.conclusion: The company could bring a suit for a declaration of its status as tenant and for prohibitory or mandatory injunctive relief to protect its possession.
issues.legal_principle: A tenant entitled to remain in possession unless evicted in due course of law may seek a declaration of tenant status and an injunction to protect possession; there is no legal bar to such relief. The Court grounded this conclusion in the tenant's continuing protection under the applicable rent-control legislation.

predicates.tenant_possession_protection_suit: The proceeding is a suit by an occupant seeking to protect possession claimed in the capacity of tenant.
predicates.tenant_entitled_to_remain_pending_lawful: The occupant's tenant status entitles them to remain in possession unless evicted through lawful proceedings.
predicates.landlord_interfered_with_possession: The landlord interfered with or threatened the occupant's possession without first obtaining lawful eviction.

issues.definition: A tenant entitled to remain until lawful eviction may seek a declaration of tenant status and injunctive relief when the landlord interferes with possession.

issues.legal_issue: The doctrine of part performance protects possession as a defence and does not displace the existing tenant status of a person already in possession who was not put into possession under the ineffective lease.
material_facts: The company was already in possession as a tenant when the parties attempted the fresh lease.
The unregistered fresh lease was ineffective, and the company was not put into possession under it.
The company sought relief on the basis of its tenant status, not under the doctrine of part performance.
issues.conclusion: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply to the company's claim; the doctrine could not be used as a sword, and the ineffective lease did not change the character of the company's pre-existing possession as tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the doctrine of part performance and may be used as a shield to defend or protect possession, not as a sword to found an affirmative claim. It was not attracted where the claimant was already in possession as tenant and had not been put into possession in part performance of the ineffective lease. The Court relied on Probodh Kumar Das v. Dantmara Tea Co. Ltd., 66 I.A. 293, and distinguished Technicians Studio P. Ltd. v. Lila Ghosh, [1978] 1 SCR 516.

rule.if: part_performance_issue_in_tenancy_dispute and tenant_already_in_possession and not possession_delivered_under_invalid_lease and claimant_seeks_to_protect_preexisting_tenancy

predicates.part_performance_issue_in_tenancy_disput: The proceeding concerns whether part performance under an ineffective lease affects claimed tenant status.
predicates.tenant_already_in_possession: The claimant was already in possession as a tenant when the parties attempted the new lease.
predicates.possession_delivered_under_invalid_lease: The claimant was put into possession in part performance of the ineffective lease.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_protect_preexisting_te: The claimant seeks to protect an existing tenancy rather than relying on part performance as the basis of the claim.

issues.definition: Part performance cannot displace an existing tenancy where the claimant was already a tenant, was not put into possession under the ineffective lease, and seeks to protect that prior tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A defective certificate for appeal does not require dismissal solely on that ground when the appeal raises a substantial question of law of general public importance.
material_facts: The appeal reached the Supreme Court on a High Court certificate that merely stated that the case was fit for appeal and did not specify the applicable constitutional category or the question to be determined.
The appeal raised a substantial question of law of general public importance.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary objection was overruled, and the appeal was not dismissed solely because the certificate was defective.
issues.legal_principle: A certificate of fitness must give adequate reasons and identify the substantial question of law or matter of importance to be determined; a certificate that does not do so is defective. The Court nevertheless declined to dismiss this appeal solely on that basis because it raised a substantial question of law of general public importance and special leave could have been granted. It relied on Article 133 of the Constitution as it then stood, Sohanlal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, [1971] 1 SCC 275, Railway Board v. Observer Publications (P) Ltd., [1972] 3 SCR 865, Nund & Samont Co. P. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, [1970] 78 ITR 268, and India Machinery Stores P. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income Tax, [1970] 78 ITR 50.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_on_high_court_ce: The proceeding is an appeal to the Supreme Court brought on a certificate granted by a High Court.
predicates.certificate_defective: The certificate does not state adequate reasons or identify the question or matter that warrants appeal.
predicates.substantial_general_public_law_question: The appeal raises a substantial question of law of general public importance.

issues.definition: An appeal supported by a defective certificate is not dismissed solely for that defect when it raises a substantial question of law of general public importance.
